title: Good vs bad "hollow" movies - Maestro vs Saltburn

commenti.body:
I haven't seen Maestro yet, looking forward to doing that this weekend.

Saltburn was certainly interesting if not a little hollow. I loved the visuals, the production design, the direction overall was very good. The characters were also pretty interesting to me. The uncanny shocking moments of Oliver's obsession were funny and felt like this this whole role was written for a female character in a way. But at the end of the day, it doesn't quite have much to say, even if you really put your subtext cap on, I don't think it really successfully said much about love, or class or privlidge or obsession... it sort of touched on a lot of things but never did anything with it.

The build up though... the build up was fantastic. I really thought we were in for a ride the first 30+ minutes. The world was built to perfection but then there was not much else that followed.

The cinematography was drop dead gorgeous. It was.... so good I went back after I watched to look at some scenes again.

I haven't seen Saltburn yet, but Maestro seemed confused to me. 

I don't like biopics, so I appreciate that it wasn't a typical becoming a great man story... But... I don't think it ever really antagonizes it's themes about art and private life vs. public life effectively because of it. Bernstein's "wants" for success are almost entirely framed against his affairs and the marriage. Which is a good story, with some memorable shots and performances - the church and the fight in particular. 

But who is this for? Bernstein fans will be disappointed... none of his most popular achievements shown (On the Town is used cleverly), one mention of Copland, Young People's Concerts mentioned in passing. 

An interest in the man? Almost nothing is explained about him. His greatness insists upon itself, but I don't think most viewers under the age of 70 are going to know just how great within the film's boundaries. 

I actually enjoyed it, but the scope of it just felt off the mark for me.

I didn’t like Maestro and loved Saltburn, but I agree that both are hollow. I think the difference, to me, is that Maestro thought it had so much to say, without really saying anything, and Saltburn knew it didn’t have anything to say, and was content with being a fun pulpy thriller. I find few things more tedious than unearned self-importance, which is my main critique of Maestro.

I walked out of both. 

I’m a classical musician. The gay men in Maestro are just used as soulless props, they have no personality. They’re an insulting device to tell the viewer, “Yeah I banged an NPC.” He didn’t stop cheating in that marriage. He was a sex pest. In current year he’d be cancelled. I actually went to a conservatory where one of his former mistresses taught at. He wrote an opera role in A Quiet Place for her. She knew how to work the system. Moved on to be the head of San Francisco Opera. So many professors had Bernstein stories. He wasn’t a nice guy, and Maestro romanticizes him. 

As for Saltburn, it takes too long to get started, then you remember the runtime. The lead actor looks both 14 and 40 at the same time. Apparently he’s 31, and he absolutely looks 31. It’s jarring. He’s playing a college freshman. The casting choice just requires too much suspension of disbelief. The director doesn’t know how to light him. He’s acting his heart out trying to play 18, costume and hair got it right. All the director had to do was light his face so he clearly didn’t look 31. Emerald Fennell doesn’t understand how to light faces. She did the same thing to Carey Mulligan in Promising Young Woman.
Too true. Even the end of Maestro is like "age and power imbalances are cool if you're Leonard Bernstein amirite."

You just get the sense the director is trying to repaint history and romanticize early on. Leonard Bernstein was a rude sex pest. Musicians don’t come forward because they don’t want to lose their jobs, and they’re either 70 years old or over, or dead. In classical music people will confide in you at times their Bernstein stories. He’s long dead. He had a great Shostakovich 5, it’s kind he did the Young People’s Concerts. But from all of the Bernstein stories musicians who worked with him confided in me, he was a mix of Madonna, Kevin Spacey, Harvey Weinstein, Chevy Chase, and Ellen. It was an honor and then often a strange ordeal to work with him. Don’t mispronounce his last name! He would flip out and ruin your whole day. “It’s not Bernstein, it’s pronounced Bernsteeeeeeeeeen.” Then you got put on the shit list.
[removed]

Exactly. When I saw the title of this post I assumed they were going to be arguing that Saltburn was the better “hollow” movie but I was surprised that they were team Maestro. Saltburn is a very stupid movie that knows how dumb it is and has a ton of fun with its concept because of it. I loved it

Really enjoyed both but I absolutely loved Maestro. Saltburn was great fun and sometimes that’s just absolutely fine for a movie. I think Maestro was really creative in its direction given I would never in a million years expect a name like Bradley Cooper to approach it that way. I think it was clear he as a writer/director/lead actor had a real love for the music and a real love for the character he was playing. I would never in a million years compare it literally to Lawrence of Arabia or Malcolm X, but like those I always find biopics with a very morally complex lead to be the most fascinating.

I think a lot people are misunderstanding what *Maestro* is supposed to be. I left the film with not much more knowledge about Bernstein than I went into the film with—but I don’t think that’s it’s aim at all and I’m glad for it. It’s so much more about his wife and family, and the complexities and struggles of loving someone so creatively gifted. More a love story than a biopic. Carey Mulligan gives the performance of the year as well—just magical—rivaled only by maybe Sandra Huller. Also Libatique’s cinematography was impeccable. 

In contrast, I completely agree that Saltburn felt utterly hollow. Probably my most disappointing film experience of the year, as I really enjoyed *Promising Young Woman* and had hoped for a better follow up. Keoghan’s performance was really great but that’s about all I felt it had to offer other than the visuals.

Yeah, neither worked for me. I probably preferred Maestro leaving me feeling "what was the point of that?" to Saltburn's "I think Emerald Fennel has completely mangled her misguided point", but definitely the two biggest disappointments of this time of year, for me.

I feel like it really works—at least for me—as a love story more than a biopic. I don’t really care that I didn’t learn much about Bernstein because I loved Mulligan and Cooper together so much. The Thanksgiving Day Parade fight was just fantastically written and I was super impressed with Libateque’s visual direction as well. Maybe the best *looking* movie I saw all year.
[removed]

Fully agree with everything said here. I left asking myself, “that’s it?”—but the first hour(?) was fantastic. The Bathtub scene was delightfully stomach churning too and I would have paid the price of admission just for the first 30 minutes at the Saltburn house. I also loved the characters, but wish it had stuck the landing.

Maestro is a by-the-books biopic where queerness is the villain, and equivocated to his narcissistic flaws. Most of the film is Carey Mulligan glaring at her husband making out with other men, or Maya Hawke begging her father not to be gay— and the film is empathising with them, presenting his queerness as an evil trait or flaw in his character, rather than vilifying the social context in which he lived that required the closet. And it even ends with him being a lecherous and predatory old man. 

At least Saltburn is *fun*.

I watched both these movies recently. Maestro is shot, produced and acted beautifully and also masterfully directed with some inspired choices. But it doesn't have anything to say, series of vignettes. 

Saltburn probably thinks it has something to say but it doesn't and arguably can't. It's a Mr. Ripley rip off with a bunch of shock scenes thrown in for the effect. The only thing I liked about this movie are the dialogues the family had among themselves.
lol all my gaffer/dp friends have the exact same criticism of saltburn

I’m sorry, but why can’t this director understand lighting? He looks a hard 31. Light him and pick a good lens. Joan Crawford famously got the best lighting. Lighting on Humoresque was so kind and courteous. It makes Saltburn infuriating. He’s a hard 31. You have to shoot him differently. Her ineptitude makes it look like a Benjamin Button scenario. Bad lighting ruins this film because the lighting makes him look too old for the part. He looks 40.

>He wasn’t a nice guy, and Maestro romanticizes him.

Maybe had you not walked out and watched the entire movie you wouldn't be saying that.

(Also, why do people actually walk out on a film? )

It appears her main visual inspiration were Caravaggio paintings ([^(ref)](https://theartgorgeous.com/saltburn-a-canvas-of-art-references-in-film/)^(/)[^(ref)](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-features/saltburn-director-emerald-fennell-creating-films-visual-style-1235683573/)), but, of course, the issue with that is exactly your point -- under-lighting or, worse, aging performers with intense shadow. I feel, the only explanation is she just didn't think/care about it.

She valued her own aesthetic over the reality/world of the film.

I feel the same as you word for word. I didn't like the end of Promising Young Woman, but I thought it was phenemonal aside from that. Likewise, I was quite disappointed in Saltburn. 

I always find it weird how people are trying to shackle Maestro with this Oscar bait or by-the-books biopic. It's a lot of things and there are criticisms, but I wouldn't call it a standard biopic. The movie's focus comes in during the Mahler piece. In that scene, you clearly realize that this is a love story and about a family, not about some creative genius. But others may disagree.

I agree that it could have delved deeper into the themes it was talking about. But just like how I appreciate this is not a standard biopic, I appreciate that the film doesn't linger too long on some things. There's a version where the Matt Bomer character keeps coming back to act as some third wheel lover, and there's a version where we show Lenny having a drug problem for 30 minutes. In the latter situation, there's simply one amusing cocaine scene that communicates everything that needs to be communicated.
Exactly?! The first thing I thought walking out of the film was how selfish Bernstein was and in some ways completely removed most of Felicia's agency.

Saltburn is style over substance movie with a good actor.

Maestro is a very good rendition of a true story with masterful acting from Bradley Cooper and Carey Mulligan. 

Every frame is weighted. Editing is perfect. Cinematography is brilliant. Story is engaging. It leaves room for the viewer to breath the story.

Honestly I wouldn't be surprised if it won best picture and Best actor in the leading role.

Even if Bernstein was not a good guy his story his worth telling. It's up to the viewer to decide if he was a moral guy according to their standards. It's funny how many movies would not exist of we only portrayed "good" ppl. Also morality is different Iin different times. It's a nice opportunity to reflect on human nature and different cultures. If we only completed it/made movies according to our era cultural code we'd be missing out on a lot of depth.

I feel we've become so binary and manicheean.

Oh I did not know about this fact about Bernstein. Wholeheartedly agree on using gay men as props. Matt Bomer hardly had 1 min screen time. Maestro absolutely felt Oscar baity to me. Cooper played pageantry for Oscars. He made movie for academy voters rather than audience. Film tried and failed to build a proper narrative but without tapping into the psyche of the artist, that asks something of director. 

Just curious, as a classical musician how’d you feel about TAR? It was completely immersive and riveting for me as an non musician.

In hindsight I liked Tár. It tells the story of a sex predator. I liked it because it felt real. It was scary. A fake person using their clout to be a sex pest. It’s funny her inspiration was Bernstein. She’s basically what Bernstein was in reality.

I agree. Like I said I do not enjoy biopics normally, and I really did enjoy this. I'm not looking for a documentary either. I just think the film doesn't begin with the same sights it ends with. 

Maybe that's due to him meeting Felicia, and there's a turn where it becomes about his "love of people." His career almost plays as meta-subtext. 

I did say I enjoyed the movie, I really just feel something was fundamentally off in where we started and where we got. A rewatch might help me gather those thoughts. Maybe I'm off the mark.

I agree it works as a love story, I just feel like the movie changes its intent halfway through. I can't articulate it well I admit.

I think the opening quote could be used for and against the film. I don't think it offers the "contradictory answers," but the first half of the film does feel contradictory to the second half: "A work of art does not answer questions, it provokes them; and its essential meaning is in the tension between the contradictory answers." 

I know I sound like a blowhard knob hater, but I really did like the movie.

Your take on both *Maestro* and *Saltburn* is quite insightful! It's always interesting to see the broad spectrum of public opinion on films, especially when critics and audiences don't always agree. 

If I may add, sometimes it feels like a "hollow" label gets slapped onto films that choose to prioritize emotion and atmosphere over complex themes or tightly woven plots. Like you said, a movie doesn’t necessarily need to have a straightforward theme to be meaningful. Sometimes inducing an emotional response or creating an engaging ambiance can be far more effective and interesting.

Coming to *Maestro*, the artistry used in depicting Bernstein's life moments might not have had a clear message or moral, but that doesn't mean it's devoid of substance. The emotional truth you felt watching it definitely validates that. I resonate with your sentiment; indeed, sometimes it's these quiet, emotive scenes that, while not grandly significant in the larger plot, stay with us far longer.

On the other hand, *Saltburn* felt like more of a big-budget aesthetic trip than a substantial storytelling experience. It had its visually captivating moments, but from your review, it seems to have sacrificed depth for surface-level intrigue.

All in all, I think what really matters are these personal connections we make with films, far more than any widespread critical consensus. After all, aren’t films supposed to stir emotions and thoughts inside us, not merely entertain us passively? This post affirms to keep an open mind and not judge a film based solely on public opinion or standard narratives, so kudos to that, mate!

I actually just watched Maestro this morning, and a movie can be both exceptionally well-crafted AND hollow at the same time. 

I felt that the soul of this movie was "Lets see how well Bradley Cooper can write, act, and direct." I mean, he can write, he can act, and he can direct. So he is going to craft a well-made movie. But when I watch a biopic, I want to know the subject of the film, I don't want to know the guy acting in it.

Even though it wasn't a biopic, I found myself comparing the movie to Tar. It is a pretty easy comparison to make. Both movies came out recently and covered similar people in similar worlds. And I just found Tar to be a lot more compelling. I know it sounds like I am being a hater, I am not. I thought Maestro was very well made. But I don't know, I thought it lacked the soul that Tar had.

Very fair! I don’t watch a TON of movies so there are definitely complexities I miss simply from not knowing the language and history quite well enough—I always like reading critical (but perhaps in your case not negative) reviews for that reason.

still need to catch Maestro. It's a little hard for me to get excited for it, Bradley Cooper is an actor who is clearly talented and I respect his career comeback and overcoming addiction and everything and i respect how very seriously he takes his craft, but also just doesnt really do anything for me (I just remembered he was the lead in *Nightmare Alley*, which I liked but also completely forgot he was in) and i am not sure if i can sit through another "gay/bi/queer man yearns too hard and wrecks his home/destroys his life" film, even partially. ~~i've done that enough in real life dont need to see it onscreen!~~

but speaking of movies about bisexuals getting into trouble, I did see Saltburn and thought it was a mess, but an entertaining one. (I saw it in theatres so the audience reaction to some of the scenes - and by some of the scenes I mean the bathtub and grave ones, you know the ones - colored it in a way that probably changed how I perceived it. I walked out thinking I watched a pulpy trashy black comedy in a "future doubleheader with Rocky Horror" sense, and everyone online was discussing it like it was *Teorema* or *Parasite*, which I think is the main issue here.)

but i do agree that it was hollow, but beyond that - so terminally a combination of both incoherent and *insistent* on doubling down on it that it was difficult for me to stay engaged beyond the relationship between Felix and Oliver. and Fernell manages to blow that one up terribly with the reveal at the end that Oliver engineered everything from the start and was scheming everything. I *loved* the twist that revealed Oliver was actually middle class, I thought the film had finally (accidentally) stumbled onto an interesting topic with regards to middle class resentment, desire, and "pretending to be poor", then it's ignored in favor of every future twist after that which just flattens Oliver and turns him into a duplicitous asshole. except that doesn't even really work either, because you're trying to tell me he was a criminal mastermind who planned this from the start right down to rigging Felix's bike? Because that doesn't really add up with the guy who was depicted prior in the film as desperate enough to interrupt him during sex with someone else like a scolded dog, who did *all that* (you know what I'm talking about) in the bathtub. i can, at the very least, maybe accept the idea that Oliver loved Felix so much that he felt the need to poison him or whatever once he felt he could no longer have him in a "i can't have him no one will" sense, not so much the powerplays to take over the entire manor for himself so he can have a naked dance scene in it by the end. like be fr. 


the closest comparison I can think of for Saltburn, is - and I realize how scathing this sounds but I genuinely mean it lovingly - is like a white gay Tyler Perry movie. pure pulp, entertaining even, great at tugging the heartstrings sometimes just because of the very high-pitched emotional mode it can careen into at times - if you go in looking for any semblance of actually anything to say or think about what actually happened on screen you will be disappointed. But also I'm like... kind of relieved as to not have to think about what Saltburn "has to say". Emerald Fennell is an private schooled oxford alum and the daughter of a famous jewelry designer and author from rich fucking Hammersmith in West London. I don't say that to suggest she's a nepo baby or anything, but because *why the fuck would you want this person of all people to weigh in on class*. She seems like a nice enough lady (albeit a filmmaker that I am becoming increasingly convinced that traffics more in [funny quips and provocation](https://www.indiewire.com/news/general-news/emerald-fennell-wants-to-make-an-erotic-jurassic-park-movie-1234929464/) over substance, which explains that headline and also the bathtub and grave scenes) but holy shit [that is not the person I want to hear from about that topic to begin with](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dI0XWAMQgxc). 

But the whole movie of Saltburn also uses class as a backdrop (but not really a theme) for the setting, so it's weird that this movie works in this weird class politics mode but also fails to say anything and instead just pisses everyone off on both sides. This is how you end up with people saying it's a movie shitting on the working class or writing screeds on letterboxd castigating its elitist, anti-working class, anti-poor politics. The movie doesn't *have* politics, that's half the problem (even if they were elitist or snobby it would at least make it more coherent in its messaging!)

There are no working class people among the main cast, not even Oliver, but again, that "btw Oliver's middle class and lying" reveal is breezed through without a care in the world so I don't fault people for belaboring this point that's an issue with Fennell with the pacing or script, because she cannot make up her mind if Saltburn is about Oliver's obsession with Felix, a comedy of manners among unreasonable circumstances skewering the rich ala *Triangle of Sadness*/*The Menu* (two other movies i found lacking in terms of trying to stick to their "eat the rich" messaging in favor of "hey did you know rich people are weird and do weird shit?"), or a slasher movie in the vein of like, "what if *The Talented Mr Ripley* was a Halloween tv special?"

I would have liked to see Julia Ducournau or Todd Haynes, (or if i'm really just throwing up dream directors here, Gregg Araki or Gus Van Sant) take a shot at this film with the same cast (because props to the cast, they probably kept this movie afloat. Keoghan is so good in this that I was willing to genuinely believe [this man](https://imgix.bustle.com/uploads/image/2023/12/26/2eceab9c-a7c0-48f9-80d6-8de73a2e536c-16saltburn1-cvmf-videosixteenbynine3000.jpg?w=414&h=478&fit=crop&crop=focalpoint&auto=format%2Ccompress&fp-x=0.4972&fp-y=0.1795) was a college freshman at least until the movie ended. it brings me no joy to admit this because I hate Sam Levinson and by extension anything *Euphoria*-related but Jacob Elordi is actually a tremendous discovery and not just a gen z pretty boy and i'm genuinely interested in his next film with Zach Quinto). But Saltburn is definitely a "get drunk and eat popcorn with the gworls" type film, it doesn't really rise to the level of anything more.

If it came out on like, Blumhouse 2/3 years ago it'd be a cult classic, but as the followup to your Best Picture-nominated, Best Screenplay Oscar debut? i dunno
also it's been a minute since i posted in this sub so if any of that is like a spoiler i can't post just let me know and i'll black it out

Why do you think that? It just showed it happened. There was no text at the bottom saying "I'm Bradley Cooper and I approve of what Bernstein is doing in this scene." If you found it gross, why is your instinct that the filmmaker DIDN'T want you to find it gross, instead of assuming it is having the intended effect? Because I'd argue the exact opposite, leaning into his self-absorbtion with the vanity license plate, the lecherous behavior, the showboating for applause in class, the REM song blasting in the car, all of these things are very intentionally assembled to make him look kind of pathetic at the end.

You're right, I hyperbolized the intent. But I don't think he's framed as pathetically as you say either. The film really only frames his behavior as negative against Felicia and his family. With that plot resolved, Bernstein is just an old man who still, as the film puts it, "loves people." 

The young man being kind of into it made me lean towards "old man still got it." As if yes, he clearly loved Felicia and his family  - but in the modern 90s he gets to live without constraint unfortunately well beyond his prime. Like he's still at it minus the eroticism. 

But you're right that if my gut feeling is "eugh" then I should trust that feeling. 

I also gotta admit I didn't realize the REM needle drop was diegetic, that's hilarious.
If Saltburn knows how dumb it is, why does it need a spoon-feeding montage in the end to break everything down?
Because it’s set up the same way as a melodramatic gothic tragic romance, so of course it has a big melodramatic tragic gothic romantic montage

I liked the melodrama and Wuthering Heights influences but it tries so hard to be a modern day gothic, that it forgets to be the “stupid” movie we all want it to be. I was gripped until that last act.
I don’t know, I found it to be pretty stupid the whole way through. But it plays it straight instead of going into comedic territory, and that’s what sells it in my opinion

Saltburn is terrible, it's just a flashy piece of glass, like a kid who has dressed up in a box of costume jewelry and faux furs. 

It doesn't even work as an effective and fun horror film. It's just...*nothing.* 

Although I must say it's not as bad as Babylon (2022). Babylon is the most expensive bag of garbage Hollywood has made recently and I am thrilled that they lost so much money even with all those "big name stars" who tried to save it.

It's another one of those "hollow" movies - and then some. At least Saltburn is somewhat true to popular culture of the period (early 2000s) while Babylon can't make up its mind if it's the 1920s or the 1970s or the late 1980s (seriously, Margot Robbie looks like a Guns n Roses groupie for the first 20 minutes of the film).

I'm probably going to stay away from Maestro until it comes on streaming if you're telling me it's one of these vapid money wasters.

You don’t consider Felix’s parents comedic territory? The mom’s performative caring? Duncan or Carey Mulligan’s character are straight out of Addams Family. The motives of the main leads are ambiguous and far from straight, which I loved. But therein lies the issue, sometimes it’s straight, sometimes it’s complex, sometimes it’s Wuthering Heights, sometimes it’s Call Me By Your Name, sometimes it’s Talented Mr. Ripley. It’s a fun yet frustrating ride with an identity crisis.
